title: Hook Fundamentals
description: Understand what Git hooks are, how they work, and which events they can hook into.

data.text: Git hooks are scripts that run automatically at key points in the Git lifecycle. They can enforce commit conventions, run tests before a push, validate commit messages, and trigger CI pipelines. Hooks run on the developer's machine and do not travel with the repository — unless managed by a tool.

data.title: Hook categories
items: **Client-side hooks** — Run on the developer's machine. Examples: pre-commit, pre-push, commit-msg.
**Server-side hooks** — Run on the Git server. Examples: pre-receive, update, post-receive.
Client-side hooks enforce local conventions. Server-side hooks enforce repository-wide policies.

data.title: Enable a sample pre-commit hook
data.code:
# Sample hooks are in .git/hooks/ with .sample extension
# To enable one, remove the .sample extension and make it executable:

mv .git/hooks/pre-commit.sample .git/hooks/pre-commit
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit

# Verify it is active
ls -l .git/hooks/pre-commit

# Test it — try to commit
git commit --allow-empty -m "test"

data.text: Hook scripts must be executable (chmod +x) and exit with code 0 to allow the operation to proceed. Any non-zero exit code aborts the operation and prints the script's output to the terminal.

data.title: Simple pre-commit hook example
data.code:
#!/bin/bash
# .git/hooks/pre-commit

echo "Running pre-commit checks..."

# Run linter
npm run lint
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Lint failed. Fix errors before committing."
  exit 1
fi

# Run tests
npm test
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Tests failed. Fix before committing."
  exit 1
fi

echo "Pre-commit checks passed."
exit 0

data.title: Hooks are local by default
data.text: The .git/hooks/ directory is not tracked by Git. To share hooks across a team, use a tool like Husky, Lefthook, or pre-commit. These tools check in hook scripts and install them during setup.

items: **exit 0** — Allow the Git operation to proceed
**exit 1** — Block the operation and display the script's stderr/stdout

items.question: Can I use any programming language for Git hooks?
items.answer: Yes, as long as the interpreter is available on the developer's machine. Shell scripts are the most portable. Python, Node.js, and PowerShell hooks are also common.

items.question: How do I disable a hook temporarily?
items.answer: Use the --no-verify (or -n) flag with the relevant Git command: git commit --no-verify, git push --no-verify. Do not make a habit of this.

items.question: Can hooks make commits slower?
items.answer: Yes, especially pre-commit hooks that run full test suites. Use fast, targeted checks in pre-commit and defer expensive operations to pre-push or CI.

items.question: Do hooks work on Windows?
items.answer: Yes, but use .bat or .ps1 extensions for native Windows compatibility. Cross-platform tools like Husky handle this automatically.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Git hooks are scripts that run at key points in the Git lifecycle
Client-side hooks run locally; server-side hooks run on the Git server
Hooks must be executable and return exit 0 to allow the operation
Return non-zero to block the operation and display an error message
Use Husky or pre-commit to share hooks across a team
